# Image to Text - Spring AI - Ollama (llava:7b)

This example demonstrates how to build a text-to-image application using a
locally hosted large language model (LLM) with [Ollama](https://ollama.com/).
Users can upload a photo, and the model will generate a descriptive response.

Ollama is an open-source platform and command-line tool that allows developers
to download, manage, and run LLMs entirely on local machines. This removes the
need for cloud APIs, access keys, and privacy-related concerns. It supports
multimodal inputs, tool calling, and integrations with REST and
[Java](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j/tree/main/langchain4j-ollama),
making it ideal for prototyping, debugging, and deploying LLM-powered
applications in an offline, customisable environment.

This example uses [Spring AI](https://spring.io/projects/spring-ai), a
Java-based framework for building applications powered by LLMs. It offers tools
for prompt management, LLM call chaining, memory handling, retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG), and integration with external data sources—all within the Java
ecosystem.

[LangChain4J](https://github.com/langchain4j/langchain4j) is an alternative
framework that also provides an abstraction layer between LLMs and the
application.

Please note that not all models can accurately describe images. For this
example, we will use [llava:7b](https://ollama.com/library/llava:7b).

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download)

- [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/)

## Run the example

1. Download and setup Ollama

   If you haven’t already, please download and install Ollama from the
   [official download page](https://ollama.com/download), following the
   instructions provided. Ollama includes a command-line tool for managing and
   interacting with it.

   Models must be downloaded from a repository, such as the
   [Ollama Library](https://ollama.com/library) or
   [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models). Ensure the model is saved in
   a supported format, such as
   [GPT-Generated Unified Format (GGUF)](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/gguf).

   To list models installed locally, run:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   After a fresh installation, no models will be listed.

   ```
   NAME    ID    SIZE    MODIFIED
   ```

   To get started, download [LLaVA](https://ollama.com/library/llava:7b) with:

   ```shell
   ollama pull llava:7b
   ```

   This process may take a few seconds to several minutes, depending on your
   internet connection.

   Once the model is downloaded, you can begin using it.

   (*Optional*) To confirm the model has been installed, list the models again:

   ```shell
   ollama list
   ```

   You should now see `llava:7b` in the list.

   ```
   NAME        ID              SIZE      MODIFIED
   llava:7b    8dd30f6b0cb1    4.7 GB    Less than a second ago
   ```

   To interact with the model using the command-line interface, run:

   ```shell
   ollama run llava:7b
   ```

   This opens a prompt where you can engage with the model. If the model has not
   yet been downloaded, Ollama will download it automatically. You can interact
   with the model via the CLI

   ```
   >>> When did humans first land on the Moon?

   Humans first landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969, during the Apollo 11 mission. The spacecraft carrying the astronauts, Neil Armstrong and Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin, landed on the lunar surface in the Sea of Tranquility at 20:17 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time). Armstrong became the first person to set foot on the Moon, famously declaring "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind" as he stepped out of the lunar module Eagle.

   >>> /bye
   ```

   Alternatively, you can interact with the model through a graphical interface,
   such as [Open WebUI](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui), which offers
   a web-based experience similar to cloud-hosted models.

   To verify that Ollama is running and accessible on the default port `11434`,
   use:

   ```shell
   curl --silent --show-error 'http://localhost:11434/api/tags' | jq
   ```

   This will return a list of available models.

   ```json
   {
     "models": [
       {
         "name": "llava:7b",
         "model": "llava:7b",
         "modified_at": "2077-04-27T11:34:56.789000000Z",
         "size": 4733363377,
         "digest": "8dd30f6b0cb19f555f2c7a7ebda861449ea2cc76bf1f44e262931f45fc81d081",
         "details": {
           "parent_model": "",
           "format": "gguf",
           "family": "llama",
           "families": [
             "llama",
             "clip"
           ],
           "parameter_size": "7B",
           "quantization_level": "Q4_0"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   When using Ollama via the REST API, as in the following steps, the required
   model must be downloaded in advance. Ollama does not automatically download
   missing models when accessed through the REST API; this functionality is only
   available via the CLI, for example with `ollama run llava:7b`. Please ensure
   the `llava:7b` model is available before proceeding.

   Verify that the Ollama APIs can be successfully invoked.

   ```shell
   # Encode the image separately to avoid oversized curl command arguments.
   base64 -i 'assets/images/Image-1.jpg' > '/tmp/image-1.b64'

   # Build the JSON request body with the prompt and encoded image.
   jq -n \
     --rawfile image '/tmp/image-1.b64' \
     --arg prompt "Describe what you see in the attached image in a sentence or two" \
     '{
       model: "llava:7b",
       prompt: $prompt,
       images: [($image | gsub("\n"; ""))],
       stream: false
     }' > '/tmp/ollama-request.json'

   # Send the prepared payload to Ollama's local generation API.
   curl 'http://localhost:11434/api/generate' \
     --silent \
     --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data @/tmp/ollama-request.json | jq

   # Remove the temporary files
   rm '/tmp/image-1.b64'
   rm '/tmp/ollama-request.json'
   ```

2. Build the application

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llava:7b` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean verify
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created and the dependencies
   copied.

   ```shell
   tree --prune --sort=name -L 1 './target'
   ```

   The application fat JAR file.

   ```
   ./target
   ├── multi-modal-springai-ollama-api-image-to-text-1.0.0.jar
   └── multi-modal-springai-ollama-api-image-to-text-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

3. Run the program

   This step assumes that Ollama is accessible on port `11434` and that the
   `llava:7b` model is available. For further details, please refer to Step 1.

   Select a photo or use one of the sample images located in the
   `./assets/images` directory.

   ```shell
   tree --sort=name './assets/images'
   ```

   Sample photos.

   ```
   ./assets/images
   ├── Image-1.jpg
   ├── Image-2.jpg
   └── Image-3.jpg

   1 directory, 3 files
   ```

   Run the example using the default image (`./assets/images/Image-1.jpg`) by
   not specifying an image path in the program.

   ![Image 1](./assets/images/Image-1.jpg)

   ```shell
   # Enable native access for classpath code because Netty loads native
   # libraries, and recent JDKs warn unless unnamed-module native access is
   # explicitly allowed.
   java \
     --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
     -jar './target/multi-modal-springai-ollama-api-image-to-text-1.0.0.jar'
   ```
